title: Architecture Standards — Master Guidelines and ADRs
author: Avery Chen
body:
Overview:

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference architecture and engineering standards. It consolidates API standards, coding guidelines, infrastructure rules, model-serving expectations, observability requirements, performance targets, and active Decision Records (ADRs). Teams should use this as the starting point for design reviews and PR checklists.

Goals:
- Ensure consistent, secure, and maintainable services across hosted, dedicated and private products.
- Provide clear, measurable performance and observability requirements for production inference workloads.
- Capture decisions that materially affect architecture, deployment, and runtime behavior.

Scope:
- Applies to all service and runtime code owned by engineering teams.
- Includes infrastructure and IaC changes that affect networking, capacity, or security posture.
- Model-serving-specific expectations for packaging, rollout, and fallbacks.

Contents (high level):
1) API Standards
2) Coding Standards and Tooling
3) Infrastructure and IaC Standards
4) Model-Serving Standards
5) Observability Standards
6) Performance Targets and Measurement
7) ADR Index and Summaries
8) Onboarding and Enforcement

1) API Standards
- Use RESTful resources for external-facing endpoints; internal microservices may use gRPC where latency and throughput justify it.
- Versioning: all external API routes MUST include a version prefix (e.g., /v1/, /v2/). Backwards-incompatible changes must be introduced under a new major version.
- Idempotency: write operations that may be retried (e.g., job creation) MUST accept an idempotency-key header and persist it with the resource.
- Authentication: use bearer tokens with short-lived client credentials for service-to-service calls; all public endpoints must authenticate via API keys scoped with minimal privileges.
- Error model: return JSON errors with schema {"code": string, "message": string, "detail": optional string}. Use standard 4xx/5xx codes; include retryable flag in trace logs for downstream routing.
- Rate limiting: implement per-API and per-customer quotas at edge; surface X-RateLimit-* headers for consumers.

API Naming & Schema Guidelines:
- Resource names are kebab-case (e.g., inference-sessions).
- Use consistent timestamp format: RFC 3339 (ISO 8601) UTC.
- Prefer explicit fields over polymorphic payloads; if polymorphism is required, use a top-level "type" discriminator.

Example endpoint contract (summary):
POST /v1/inference/sessions
Request: {
  "model": "redwood-alpha-1",
  "input": "...",
  "options": {"temperature": 0.2}
}
Response: {
  "session_id": "...",
  "status": "queued",
  "created_at": "2026-12-15T10:00:00Z"
}

2) Coding Standards and Tooling
- Language preferences: Python for orchestration and SDKs, Go for high-throughput services, and C++/CUDA for runtime kernels.
- Mandatory checks: all repositories must include linting, static type checks (mypy/TypeScript/Go vet), and unit tests in CI.
- Test coverage: critical runtime and routing code should maintain >= 70% unit coverage; other services target >= 50%.
- PR size guidance: prefer small, reviewable PRs (< 400 lines of change); include design summary for larger changes.
- Style guides: follow PEP8 for Python, Effective Go conventions, and the company ESLint/Prettier config for TypeScript.
- Security checks: incorporate SAST (e.g., semgrep) and dependency scanning in the pipeline.

Required CI Matrix:
- Lint
- Unit tests with coverage
- Integration smoke tests against a simulated runtime (for model-serving components)
- Build and publish of container images with immutable tags (git-sha)

3) Infrastructure and IaC Standards
- IaC: Terraform is the standard for cloud resources; Helm charts for Kubernetes apps. Changes to shared networking, VPCs, or IAM require a design review and approval from eng-infra.
- Naming conventions: resources use the format: rd-<env>-<team>-<service>-<purpose> (e.g., rd-prod-engserv-runtime-gpu-pool).
- Environment parity: dev/stage/prod must mirror major network and security controls; stage must use representative instance types and quantized images for performance testing.
- Secrets: must be stored in supported KMS (AWS KMS / GCP KMS / HashiCorp Vault). No secrets in code or plaintext.
- Capacity: GPU fleets must include headroom for 20% burst above 95th percentile demand; autoscaling policies must use both GPU utilization and request queue depth signals.

Network Security Checklist:
1. Restrict control-plane endpoints to management networks and IP allowlists for private customers.
2. Enforce TLS1.2+ for all internal and external traffic.
3. Use mTLS for service-to-service authentication where PKI support exists.

Example Terraform snippet (network tagging):
```hcl
resource "aws_security_group" "runtime_sg" {
  name = "rd-prod-engserv-runtime-sg"
  tags = {
    Environment = "prod"
    Team = "engserv"
    Service = "runtime"
  }
}
```

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Model packaging: models must be versioned with semantic versioning and include a manifest.json with fields: model_name, version, quantization_profile, required_kernels, input_schema.
- Quantization profiles: teams must publish quantization profiles under confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles with performance/quality tradeoffs.
- KV cache semantics: runtime should expose hooks for client libraries to warm or pin prefixes; documentation must state cache eviction semantics.
- Rollout strategies: use canary (10% traffic for 30 minutes) followed by progressive rollout (doubling traffic every 30-60 minutes) for model and runtime releases. Automated rollback triggers: >5% error rate increase or >10% latency regression sustained for 10 minutes.
- Compatibility: when changing tokenizer or input-schema, support a compatibility shim or bump major model version and notify downstream owners.

Model Deployment Checklist:
- Model artifact signed and checksum verified.
- Manifest present and validated in CI.
- End-to-end smoke test against canonical prompt set.
- Observability metrics included (latency buckets, request rate, error rate, token count).

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics: emit OpenMetrics-compatible counters/gauges/histograms with standard labels: service, team, env, model, route.
- Required metrics:
  - inference_requests_total{status, model, route}
  - inference_latency_seconds_bucket (p50/p90/p95/p99)
  - tokens_generated_total
  - cache_hit_ratio
  - gpu_utilization_percent
- Tracing: use W3C tracecontext; spans must annotate model name, model_version, route, and sampling decision.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with level, timestamp, request_id, trace_id, and semantic fields. PII must be redacted before logging.
- Alerts: define SLO-based alerts (see section 6). Alert routing: PagerDuty for SLO breaches, Slack for degraded warnings.

6) Performance Targets and Measurement
- Global target for hosted API (default model small-medium seq=512):
  - p50 latency <= 40ms (generation token step)
  - p95 latency <= 150ms
  - p99 latency <= 400ms
  - throughput per GPU varies by model; teams must publish baseline throughput numbers in the model catalog.
- SLOs (examples):
  - Availability: 99.9% (monthly) for hosted inference routes.
  - Model-serving error rate: <0.5% (5xxs) on rolling 30d window.
- Measurement: use synthetic load tests in stage with production-like request distribution. Capture token distribution and prefix lengths for realistic batching.

Performance Testing Procedure (brief):
1. Deploy candidate runtime/model to stage with representative instance types.
2. Run perf harness capturing latency histograms and tail behavior under load.
3. Validate cost-per-token and throughput against target.
4. If regression >10% vs baseline, open a regression-triage ticket and block rollout.

7) ADR Index and Summaries
- ADR-2025-01: Standardize on Terraform + Helm for IaC and K8s templating. Decision: adopt Terraform for cloud resources and Helm for application packaging. Rationale: reuse existing infra automation and better lifecycle control.
- ADR-2026-03: Model artifact manifest and semantic versioning. Decision: require manifest.json and semantic versioning for every model release. Rationale: simplifies rollout automation and compatibility checks.
- ADR-2026-07: Default to gRPC internal surface for high-throughput routing. Decision: allow internal high-throughput routes to use gRPC; external public API remains REST. Rationale: lower CPU overhead and uniformity for high-ql services.
- ADR-2026-10: Production fallback policy. Decision: require at least two compatible model variants (primary + cheaper fallback) for each hosted route. Rationale: preserve availability during capacity shortages.

Each ADR includes: status, author, date, status of action items, and related tickets. Full ADRs are maintained under confluence/architecture-and-standards/adrs/ (see related_pages).

8) Onboarding and Enforcement
- New design proposals must include a checklist mapping to the sections above.
- Architecture reviews: all changes that touch networking, data residency, or model serving must be reviewed by platform and security.
- Automated checks: CI should validate API schema contracts (OpenAPI) and manifest presence for models.
- Exceptions: documented through the risk-and-exceptions flow and require approver from security or eng-infra depending on impact.

Appendix: Example model manifest.json
```json
{
  "model_name": "redwood-alpha-1",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "quantization_profile": "q4_0",
  "required_kernels": ["attention_v2", "prefetch_kv"],
  "input_schema": {"type": "string", "max_length": 2048}
}
```

Contact and ownership:
- Document owner: eng-architecture (Avery Chen).
- Review cadence: annually or when a major platform change occurs.
- For questions: tag @eng-architecture in the internal RFC channel.

Change log (high level):
- 2026-03-01: Initial consolidation of standards.
- 2026-06-15: Added rollout and fallback policy (ADR-2026-10).
- 2026-12-15: Added performance target clarifications and expanded ADR index.
